Panic Disorder and Its Mimics: Which Anxiety, and How to Treat

Are the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Exclude a substance and a medical cause first:

  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), glucose and urine toxicology
  • Consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) for palpitations or chest pain

No test makes the diagnosis.

Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks, then 1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behavior.

Attacks only in feared social situations, or with one feared object or situation, are social anxiety disorder or specific phobia.

Treat with CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both. Start the drug low and titrate slowly.

A benzodiazepine is short term only.

Diagnosis
Panic disorder criteria A – recurrent unexpected panic attacks; each an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort, peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms (STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's) · B – at least 1 month, after at least 1 attack, of persistent worry about more attacks or their consequences, or a significant maladaptive change in behavior related to the attacks · C – not attributable to a substance or another medical condition · D – not better explained by another mental disorder
STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's
  • S – sweating
  • T – trembling
  • U – unsteadiness, dizziness
  • D – depersonalization, derealization
  • E – excessive heart rate, palpitations
  • N – nausea
  • T – tingling
  • S – shortness of breath
  • FEAR – of dying, of losing control, of going crazy
  • C – chest pain, chills, choking
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineCBT with exposure, an SSRI or venlafaxine XR, or bothDrug ineffective after at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range
Second lineClomipramine, imipramine or mirtazapine; a benzodiazepine (short term)Top rung
By situation Starting the SSRI – half the usual depression starting dose; increase about every 7 days (early activation makes patients stop it) · Severe symptoms or co-existing conditions before the SSRI works – a benzodiazepine such as alprazolam until the antidepressant takes effect; short term only · History of substance use – avoid benzodiazepines; gabapentin and mirtazapine are recommended · Not recommended – propranolol; buspirone (helps generalized anxiety; does not appear effective for panic disorder) · Improved – continue the drug for 12 months, then taper
Follow-up Response – with some meaningful improvement at 4 to 6 weeks, allow several months before judging the full effect · Watch for – depression and disability, alcohol and substance use, suicidal ideation, all more common in panic disorder; agoraphobia often co-occurs
Practice
  1. 32-year-old woman, 8 months of episodes racing heart, sweating, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; some at rest 7 months avoiding buses, crowds, lines: no escape or help oriented, anxious about the next · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, toxicology normal → Panic disorder and agoraphobia → unexpected attacks plus fear of 2 or more situations where escape is hard; when criteria for both are met, both are assigned
  2. 41-year-old man, 9 months of worry, more days than not about job, finances, children's safety; cannot switch it off restless, tired, tense; sleeps poorly No sudden episodes of intense fear alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH normal → Generalized anxiety disorder → excessive worry about a number of events, hard to control, more days than not for at least 6 months, with at least 3 of 6 symptoms; the worry is not about attacks
  3. 23-year-old man, 10 months of pounding heart, sweating, shaking only when presenting in class or eating in the cafeteria fears others will see him blush, think him foolish now skips those classes alert, oriented, euthymic · afebrile; vitals, toxicology normal → Social anxiety disorder → the attacks come only in social situations, and the fear is of negative evaluation, not of the attacks
  4. 27-year-old woman, 1 year of intense fear, sweating, racing heart begins within seconds whenever she must ride an elevator climbs 12 flights of stairs to avoid it No episodes at other times alert, oriented, euthymic · vital signs normal → Specific phobia → one situation almost always provokes immediate fear and is avoided; one situation is not the 2 of 5 that agoraphobia needs
  5. 36-year-old woman, 14 months of fear that she has heart disease checks her pulse many times a day has seen three cardiologists No sudden fear episodes; occasional mild chest tightness alert, oriented, anxious, not delusional · afebrile; vitals, ECG, echocardiogram normal → Illness anxiety disorder → persistent preoccupation with a serious illness for at least 6 months with mild or no symptoms; health anxiety in panic disorder is acute and episodic
  6. 29-year-old woman, 3 months of feeling anxious and shaky, with palpitations lost 5 kg (11 lb) without trying feels hot when others are comfortable alert, oriented, restless · HR 112/min · BP 138/70 mm Hg · warm, moist skin · fine hand tremor → Serum TSH → weight loss, heat intolerance and resting tachycardia point to hyperthyroidism; a low TSH screens, and a high free thyroxine confirms
  7. 38-year-old man, 4 months of spells pounding headache, drenching sweats, racing heart each lasts 15 to 30 minutes Alert, oriented, euthymic BP 196/112 mm Hg in a spell, 150/94 between · HR 104/min · TSH 2.1 μU/mL · glucose 96 mg/dL → Plasma free metanephrines → episodes of severe hypertension with headache, sweating and a racing heart point to pheochromocytoma
  8. 22-year-old man, 2 months of sudden episodes racing heart, lightheadedness and fear they start and stop abruptly Alert, oriented, euthymic HR 76/min and BP 122/78 mm Hg between episodes · TSH, glucose and urine toxicology normal → Electrocardiogram → palpitations call for an ECG to look for preexcitation before the episodes are called panic attacks
  9. 26-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; 3 months worrying about the next wants a diagnostic test oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, ECG, toxicology normal → Sertraline at a low starting dose and CBT → criteria are met and the mimics are excluded; no test makes the diagnosis, and a lactate challenge has no standardized criteria
  10. 34-year-old man, 6 months of recurrent unexpected episodes intense fear with sweating, palpitations, dizziness, trembling stopped driving 5 months ago, fearing another asks for something to stop them alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → Escitalopram, started low and titrated → an SSRI is first line; a benzodiazepine alone does not improve longer-term outcomes, and propranolol is not recommended
  11. 28-year-old woman, 5 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, chest pain, fear of losing control months of worry started sertraline 50 mg daily 5 days ago now jittery, more anxious; wants to stop oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 88/min → Lower the dose, then raise it slowly → initial activation can be troubling; start at half the usual depression dose and increase about every 7 days
  12. 31-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying months of worry sertraline 25 mg daily for 2 weeks: little change No adverse effects alert, oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 78/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Raise the sertraline dose → a drug is not ineffective until it has been given for at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range
  13. 25-year-old man, 2 months of unexpected fear episodes palpitations, choking, sweating, chest pain; many a day housebound 6 weeks; cannot work started sertraline yesterday No substance use history oriented · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → A benzodiazepine for the first weeks → with severe symptoms, a benzodiazepine such as alprazolam bridges until the antidepressant takes effect; short term only
  14. 40-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, abstinent 2 months 5 months of recurrent unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying avoids leaving home alone alert, oriented, euthymic · vitals, TSH, ECG normal · urine toxicology negative → Alprazolam → benzodiazepines are avoided with a history of substance use; gabapentin and mirtazapine are recommended
  15. 33-year-old woman treated with sertraline and CBT for recurrent unexpected episodes of fear no episodes for 3 months asks to stop the drug alert, euthymic · HR 70/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Continue it for 12 months, then taper → once symptoms improve, continue the drug for 12 months before tapering to limit relapse
How NBME framed it: question 1

25-year-old woman, 2 months of sudden anxiety episodes, several times a week chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations fears losing control and going crazy says they come out of the blue Not depressed; sleep and appetite unchanged 170 cm, 60 kg, BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · pulse 88/min · BP 130/86 mm Hg · physical and mental status examinations normal · laboratory studies normal · urine toxicology negative

Which abnormality is she most likely to have?

Competing answers
  • Abnormal eye tracking: “going crazy” suggests psychosis; but abnormal eye tracking goes with schizophrenia, and her mental status examination is normal.
  • Delayed rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on polysomnography: the stem mentions sleep; but it goes with sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder and some drugs and alcohol, not panic disorder.
  • Enlarged third and lateral ventricles on head CT (computed tomography): a structural brain cause; but aqueductal stenosis, the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus, is atypical in a healthy young adult and does not explain the attacks.
  • Cortisol not suppressed by 1 mg of dexamethasone: a stress-axis test; but nonsuppression points to Cushing syndrome, not panic disorder.

Down to two: increased sensitivity to lactate infusions or cortisol nonsuppression. Lactate: recurrent attacks that come out of the blue, with a normal workup, point to panic disorder (NBME's key), and patients with it have attacks in response to lactate at an increased rate (the explanation ties this to catastrophic appraisal of body states). Its diagnostic utility is unclear: there are no standardized criteria. The stem never states worry or avoidance, and the lead-in asks for a finding, not the diagnosis.

Pairs with Secondary Hypertension: is the blood pressure severely high during the episodes? Thyroid Mimics & Discriminators: constant symptoms with weight loss? SSRI (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor) Adverse Effects: did the restlessness start with the drug? Bipolar Disorder: episodes of elevated mood?
Transferable rule

Exclude a substance and a medical cause first. Then name what the fear is about: the attacks themselves, negative evaluation, one object or situation, difficult escape, a number of events, or a serious illness.
